additional_tech: embed: the official 2020-12 meta-schema and vocabulary meta-schemas are compiled into the binary. The compiled meta-schema and the built-in registry index are each built exactly once per process by one shared builder and reused, never rebuilt per Compile

Exact JSON number model in internal/jsonvalue: values that fit exactly use a native int64 or float64 fast path, and math/big (big.Int / big.Rat) takes over whenever exactness requires it. The inline mantissa and exponent can be read without allocating, so multipleOf decides divisibility with int64 integer arithmetic on the common path (never floats, ADR-004) and falls back to math/big for big mantissas or huge exponents
regexp (RE2) behind a small ECMA-262-to-RE2 translation step, with deviations documented
go test with table-driven, spec-derived test cases stored as testdata JSON files
Go benchmarks (testing.B, compared with go test -count=10 and medians) and allocation-limit tests (testing.AllocsPerRun), using the standard library only

Golden CLI output files captured from the unchanged v1.1 code (commit f35d9e4) in testdata/golden/, covering flag, basic, detailed and verbose. Generated large documents are recorded there as size plus SHA-256
api_style: Go library API: compile once (registry, limits and format mode fixed at compile time), then Schema.Validate(instance) returns an immutable Result. The Result can be rendered to the 2020-12 output formats, and its annotations are flattened and sorted lazily under sync.Once on the first Annotations() or Output() call. The CLI is `jsonschema validate` with flags for the schema file, registry files and directories mapped to base URIs, output format, format assertion and limits. Documents come from file paths or stdin. With one document, stdout is exactly one output-format JSON object. With several, it prints one labelled JSON report per line, and the worst result sets the exit code.
architecture_style: Keyword plug-in modules behind a small registry. Package `jsonschema` (root) holds the public API: Compiler/Options, Schema, Validate, Result and OutputUnit. Internal packages hold the engine pieces: internal/jsonvalue (exact number model with a small-number fast path, allocation-free mantissa/exponent access, deep equality), internal/uri (RFC 3986 resolution, JSON Pointer), internal/registry (resource index, $id, $anchor, $dynamicAnchor, and embedded meta-schemas with one shared built-in index builder), internal/compile (schema compilation, vocabulary handling, limits, the meta-schema cache, and static analysis that marks whether a subschema needs evaluated-location or annotation tracking), internal/eval (evaluation, with a per-call stack of path frames indexed by depth, an embedded lazy location, dynamic scope with explicit exit calls, chunked annotation collection and unevaluated* tracking only where needed), internal/keywords/<vocabulary> (one file per keyword, each registering itself, with a per-call collector that keeps one reusable child EvalContext per depth), internal/formats (one file per format, each registering itself) and internal/output (flag/basic/detailed/verbose, with copy-free pointer rendering and a pre-sized report buffer). There is a thin CLI in cmd/jsonschema.
auth_model: none (local library and CLI; no accounts)
conventions: Each keyword lives in its own file internal/keywords/<vocabulary>/<keyword>.go with its own <keyword>_test.go. It registers itself from an init() call into the keyword registry (internal/keywords/registry.go), giving its name, vocabulary URI, compile function and evaluate function. No central keyword list or switch is ever edited to add a keyword. Each vocabulary package is pulled in once by a single blank import in internal/keywords/all/all.go. Formats (internal/formats/<format>.go) and output shapes (internal/output/<shape>.go) register the same way. cmd/jsonschema/main.go only parses flags and calls the root package.

go.mod has no require lines and stays that way in this round. Adding any dependency needs an explicit operator decision. Go discovers new files in a package folder without any manifest edit, so a story adds its new code and tests as new files rather than growing shared ones.

Spec-derived tests are written by this project and kept as JSON cases in testdata/<area>/<keyword>.json, one file per keyword or behaviour, with a shared table-driven runner. Each test cites the 2020-12 core or validation spec section it derives from.

Performance changes keep results identical: the same valid/invalid answer, the same flag/basic/detailed/verbose reports, the same library Result, error messages, limits, exit codes and goroutine safety. No existing test is removed or weakened, and go test -race stays green.

CLI golden files in testdata/golden/ are captured once from v1.1 (f35d9e4) in the first task of round-3 story 1, before any production code changes, and committed with that story. They cover the perf fixtures, docs/examples and the testdata cases in all four output formats (stdout, stderr and exit code). No later story may regenerate or edit a golden file. A story whose output differs from a golden file has failed and stops.

Per-call reuse invariants are documented next to the code and tested. A path frame (internal/eval) is valid only while its node is being evaluated, and frames are entered and left strictly last-in first-out through explicit exit calls, never closures. A child EvalContext from EvalChild must not be kept by any keyword after EvalChild returns, and the caller owns the returned units slice. Annotation chunks grow 16, 32, … up to 4,096 entries and roll back by mark and truncate.

Every number rule (type integer, multipleOf, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, enum, const, uniqueItems) has tests covering both the native fast path and the exact math/big path, including the boundary between them. The multipleOf int64 path has a random differential test against the big path over at least 1 M inputs, and an AllocsPerRun test proving 0 allocations on small numbers.

Performance guards live in their own files: benchmarks in <package>/bench_test.go and allocation-limit tests in <package>/allocs_test.go, one pair per package measured. Each limit is the measured count after the change plus about 10% headroom, recorded next to the test with the measured value, and is lowered on purpose by each story as docs/benchmarks.md describes. A new randomised or counter test goes in its own new _test.go file.

Each story records benchmark medians before and after (go test -bench -count=10 on the same machine) in docs/benchmarks.md. The targets come from one Apple M3 Max with Go 1.27.2; on other hardware they are compared relative to the before numbers. A missed target is reported and the story is held for the operator's decision, never merged as done silently.

CLI peak memory is measured only by the opt-in TestCLIPeakMemory in cmd/jsonschema (-peakmem flag, unix only, skipped by default) and /usr/bin/time -l on the built CLI, with before and after values recorded in docs/benchmarks.md. No default test run depends on peak memory or timings.

Performance fixtures: the order schema and the 0.5 KB order document are stored in testdata/perf/. The large documents (about 0.5 MB, about 0.33 MB with 1,000 errors, and about 5.5 MB) are generated in Go code (internal/perfdata) from a fixed, seed-free recipe, so they are identical on every run and never committed.

The compiled Schema and everything reachable from it are immutable after Compile returns. Per-evaluation state (path frame stack, child contexts, dynamic scope, annotation chunks, evaluated locations, limit counters) lives in a per-call evaluation context and is never shared between calls, enforced by tests run with go test -race.

Documentation lives in docs/: regex deviations from ECMA-262, the list of partly checked formats (including idn-hostname and idn-email), the CLI contract, the default limits, and docs/benchmarks.md (how to run the benchmarks, the measured numbers and how allocation limits are set).
deployment: Distributed as a Go module (go get) and as a single static CLI binary built with `go build ./cmd/jsonschema`. No network access at build, test or run time beyond the standard Go toolchain.
description: A JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 validator written from scratch in Go. It has two parts: a Go library (load a schema once, then check many documents with it, safely from several goroutines) and a non-interactive command-line tool. It works fully offline. Remote references are resolved only through a caller-supplied schema registry, with the official 2020-12 meta-schema and vocabulary meta-schemas embedded in the binary. It reports the 2020-12 output formats (flag, basic, detailed, verbose), with basic as the default. Exit codes are 0 valid, 1 invalid and 2 tool, usage or schema error. Reports give the failing location and rule, never the instance value. Format is an annotation by default and an assertion in an optional mode. Built-in limits protect against hostile inputs. Performance round 3 cuts memory and time further, one story each and in this order: (1) reuse evaluation path frames; (2) one child evaluation context per depth; (3) object keywords without wasted copies; (4) annotations collected in growing chunks; (5) render the report without copies; (6) multipleOf without big integers on the common path; (7) build the built-in meta-schema index once. Validation behaviour, output, exit codes, limits, error messages and goroutine safety do not change at all.
forbidden: Any existing JSON Schema validation library as a dependency, for example santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema, xeipuuv/gojsonschema, qri-io/jsonschema, google/jsonschema-go or kaptinlin/jsonschema
Referencing, importing or benchmarking against santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema (tekuri) or any other validator inside the project: the comparison stays outside it
Copying, vendoring, downloading or referencing the official JSON-Schema-Test-Suite, Bowtie or any copy of them
Network access of any kind at build, test or run time (no HTTP fetching of $ref targets)
Reading files from disk other than those the caller explicitly supplied (no file:// resolution on its own)
Including instance values in error output or logs
Third-party dependencies in go.mod without an explicit operator decision (this includes golang.org/x/net/idna, which the operator declined)
Support for JSON Schema drafts other than 2020-12
Mutating a compiled Schema after Compile returns
Changing any validation result, output report, library Result, error message, limit behaviour, exit code or goroutine-safety guarantee as part of a performance change
Regenerating, editing or updating a CLI golden file after it is captured from v1.1
Removing or weakening any existing test
Floating-point arithmetic in the multipleOf decision
Fixed-size annotation chunks (growing chunk sizes 16 … 4,096 are required)
Keeping a path frame or a child EvalContext beyond the evaluation of its node or the EvalChild call
Committing the large generated performance documents to the repository
Timing-based or peak-memory-based assertions in default test runs (speed is measured by benchmarks only, while tests check allocation counts)
framework: none (Go standard library only: encoding/json with UseNumber and Decoder for streaming tokens, math/big, regexp, net/url, unicode, embed, flag, sort, sync, testing)
name: jsonschema-2020-12
nfrs: Fully offline: the validator never fetches a URI and never reads a file the caller did not list. Unresolvable references are an error with exit code 2.

Hostile-input safe: limits on nesting depth, $ref/$dynamicRef recursion depth, evaluation steps, input size and report bytes, with generous defaults that callers can raise through a library option and a CLI flag. Exceeding a limit is an error with exit code 2. The report-bytes limit fails at exactly the same point as in v1.1. Regex is RE2, which runs in linear time.

Exact JSON number semantics: 1.0 is an integer, multipleOf is exact on decimals, and big integers and decimals keep full precision. The small-number fast path never changes an answer and never uses floating-point arithmetic for multipleOf.
String length counts Unicode code points. uniqueItems, enum and const use deep JSON equality.
Output reports never contain instance values, only instance locations, keyword locations and error messages.
A compiled schema is safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines.
A schema that fails meta-schema validation or uses an unknown required vocabulary is an error (exit code 2), never 'invalid'.
The CLI exit codes are a contract: 0 valid, 1 invalid, 2 error. With several documents, the worst result wins.
CLI stdout, stderr and exit code stay byte-identical to v1.1 (f35d9e4) in flag, basic, detailed and verbose, checked against committed golden files.

Round-3 targets (Apple M3 Max, Go 1.27.2; elsewhere relative to before): story 1 Validate5_5MB at most 280 MB and 4.8 M allocs/op, ValidateErrors at most 22.5 MB, CompileOrder at most 1,600 allocs/op, no scenario more than 5% slower by median; story 2 Validate5_5MB at most 305 MB alone (200 MB with story 1), ValidateErrors at most 24.5 MB, ValidateSmall at most 35,500 B/op; story 3 Validate5_5MB at most 345 MB and 6.0 M allocs/op alone; story 4 Validate5_5MB at most 342 MB alone, ValidateErrors at most 27.4 MB, ValidateSmall at most 42,000 B/op; story 5 BenchmarkCLI/5.5MB at most 7.3 M allocs/op and 450 MB, CLI peak RSS with -o basic on 5.5 MB at least 30 MiB lower; story 6 evalMultipleOf 0 allocs on small numbers, Validate5_5MB at most 6.25 M allocs/op alone; story 7 exactly one built-in index build per process, plus a separate first-compile measure.
Verbose output keeps its current behaviour (a second evaluation pass) this round.
Overall performance goal: roughly match tekuri in speed, memory and schema loading time, checked only by the operator's separate comparison outside the project.
